q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: In 1918, women over the age of 30 were given voting rights and the right to stand for Parliament, partly in recognition of the contribution women made to the war effort during the First World War. Shortly before Emmeline Pankhurst's death in 1928, women were given the right to vote at the age of 21, the same as men.
o: In 1918 women over 30 were given voting rights, and in 1928 women could vote at 21
In 1918 women over 21 were given voting rights, and in 1928 women could vote at 30

q.t: The present voting age of 18 was set in which year?
q.e: The UK has had a fully democratic voting system since 1928. The present voting age of 18 was set in 1969 and, with a few exceptions, all UK-born and naturalised adult citizens have the right to vote.

q.t: Which TWO forms of protest did the suffragettes of the WSPU use?
q.e: Emmeline Pankhurst co-founded the Women's Social and Political Union in 1903. This was the first group whose members were called suffragettes. The group used civil disobedience as part of their protest, and many of the women went on hunger strike.

q.t: Which group did Emmeline Pankhurst set up in 1889, and what did it fight for?
q.e: Emmeline Pankhurst was born in Manchester in 1858. She set up the Women's Franchise League in 1889, which fought to get the vote in local elections for married women.
o: The Women's Franchise League, fighting for the vote in local elections for married women
The Women's Social and Political Union, fighting for the vote in local elections
The Chartists, fighting for the working man's vote
The Women's Franchise League, fighting for the vote in General Elections

q.t: Before 1870, what happened to a woman's earnings and property when she married?
q.e: In common with the rest of Europe, women in 19th century Britain had fewer rights than men. Until 1870, when a woman got married, her earnings, property and money automatically belonged to her husband. Acts of Parliament in 1870 and 1882 gave wives the right to keep their own earnings and property.
o: They automatically belonged to her husband
They were held in trust by the courts
They passed to her eldest son

q.t: What did the Reform Act of 1867 do?
q.e: Campaigners, called the Chartists, presented petitions to Parliament. At first they seemed to be unsuccessful, but in 1867 there was another Reform Act. This created many more urban seats in Parliament and reduced the amount of property that people needed to have before they could vote.
o: It created more urban seats and reduced the property needed to vote
It gave the vote to all women over 30
It abolished the pocket and rotten boroughs
It made MPs paid for the first time

q.t: What is democracy, according to the handbook?
q.e: Democracy is a system of government where the whole adult population gets a say. This might be by direct voting or by choosing representatives to make decisions on their behalf.
o: A system of government where the whole adult population gets a say
A system where only property owners may vote
A system where the monarch chooses the government
A system where judges make the laws

q.t: At the turn of the 19th century, who was able to vote in elections for members of Parliament?
q.e: At the turn of the 19th century, Britain was not a democracy as we know it today. Although there were elections to select members of Parliament, only a small group of people could vote. They were men who were over 21 years of age and who owned a certain amount of property.
o: Men over 21 who owned a certain amount of property

q.t: Which TWO changes did the Chartists want, besides the vote for every man?
q.e: In the 1830s and 1840s, a group called the Chartists campaigned for reform. They wanted six changes: for every man to have the vote, elections every year, for all regions to be equal in the electoral system, secret ballots, for any man to be able to stand as an MP, and for MPs to be paid.
o: For all regions to be equal in the electoral system

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
The UK has had a fully democratic voting system since 1928.
q.e: The UK has had a fully democratic voting system since 1928. The present voting age of 18 was set in 1969 and, with a few exceptions, all UK-born and naturalised adult citizens have the right to vote.

q.t: At what age can a person drive a car, and at what age a moped?
q.e: In the UK, you must be at least 17 years old to drive a car or motor cycle and you must have a driving licence to drive on public roads. You need to be at least 16 years old to ride a moped.
o: 17 for a car and 16 for a moped
16 for a car and 17 for a moped
18 for a car and 16 for a moped
17 for a car and 17 for a moped

q.t: Until what age is a driving licence valid, and how often must it be renewed after that?
q.e: Drivers can use their driving licence until they are 70 years old. After that, the licence is valid for three years at a time.
o: Until 70, then it is valid for three years at a time
Until 75, then it is valid for three years at a time
Until 70, then it is valid for one year at a time
Until 65, then it is valid for five years at a time

q.t: Which TWO tests must be passed to get a UK driving licence?
q.e: To get a UK driving licence you must pass a driving test, which tests both your knowledge and your practical skills. You will need to pass a driving theory test, which consists of a multiple choice theory test and a hazard perception test, and a practical driving test.

q.t: In Northern Ireland, what must a newly qualified driver display, and for how long?
q.e: In Northern Ireland, a newly qualified driver must display an 'R' plate, for restricted driver, for one year after passing the test.

q.t: For how long may a driving licence from a country outside the EU, Iceland, Liechtenstein or Norway be used in the UK?
q.e: If your driving licence is from a country in the European Union, Iceland, Liechtenstein or Norway, you can drive in the UK for as long as your licence is valid. If you have a licence from any other country, you may use it in the UK for up to 12 months.
o: For as long as the licence is valid

q.t: At what age does a vehicle need an annual MOT test?
q.e: If your vehicle is over three years old, you must take it for a Ministry of Transport (MOT) test every year. It is an offence not to have an MOT certificate if your vehicle is more than three years old.
o: When it is over three years old
When it is over one year old
When it is over ten years old
When it is over five years old

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
It is a serious criminal offence to drive without insurance.
q.e: If you are resident in the UK, your car or motor cycle must be registered at the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency. You must pay an annual road tax and you must also have valid motor insurance. It is a serious criminal offence to drive without insurance.

q.t: Which TWO charities named in the handbook work with homeless people?
q.e: They include charities working with older people, such as Age UK, with children, for example the NSPCC, and with the homeless, for example Crisis and Shelter.

q.t: Which charity named in the handbook works with animals?
q.e: There are also medical research charities, for example Cancer Research UK, environmental charities, including the National Trust and Friends of the Earth, and charities working with animals, such as the People's Dispensary for Sick Animals (PDSA).

q.t: Which programme gives 16- and 17-year-olds the opportunity to enjoy outdoor activities and take part in a community project?
q.e: There are many opportunities for young people to volunteer and receive accreditation which will help them to develop their skills. These include the National Citizen Service programme, which gives 16- and 17-year-olds the opportunity to enjoy outdoor activities, develop their skills and take part in a community project.

q.t: Which TWO roles can you volunteer for with the police?
q.e: You can volunteer with the police, and become a special constable or a lay, non-police, representative. You can also apply to become a magistrate.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: Volunteering is working for good causes without payment. There are many benefits to volunteering, such as meeting new people and helping make your community a better place. Some volunteer activities will give you a chance to practise your English or develop work skills.
o: Volunteering is working for good causes without payment
Volunteering is paid work carried out for a charity

q.t: Which TWO of these are ways of being a good neighbour, according to the handbook?
q.e: You can help prevent any problems and conflicts with your neighbours by respecting their privacy and limiting how much noise you make. Also try to keep your garden tidy, and only put your refuse bags and bins on the street or in communal areas if they are due to be collected.
o: Limiting how much noise you make
Feeding their pets without being asked
Parking in front of their house

q.t: Which of these is NOT listed in the handbook as a shared value and responsibility?
q.e: These values and responsibilities include: to obey and respect the law; to be aware of the rights of others and respect those rights; to treat others with fairness; to behave responsibly; to help and protect your family; to respect and preserve the environment; to treat everyone equally; to work to provide for yourself and your family; to help others; and to vote in local and national government elections.
o: To respect and preserve the environment
To vote in local and national government elections
